profile.name: Muixeranga
profile.tagline: A traditional Valencian performance of street dance and figurative human towers.
profile.insight: The Muixeranga is a living, plastic choreography where human towers are not built for height, but to create symbolic, figurative scenes honoring the Virgin of Health.
profile.profile: The Muixeranga is a collective tradition of street dance and human towers originating in the Kingdom of Valencia, Spain, and preserved primarily in the town of Algemesí. It combines acrobatic, choreographic, and religious elements, serving as a foundational ancestor to the modern Catalan castells. Unlike competitive human towers, the Muixeranga focuses on the creation of complex, symbolic plastic figures during the annual Mare de Déu de la Salut festival.
profile.profile_long:
The Muixeranga is a multifaceted tradition centered in the town of Algemesí, where it is performed annually on September 7 and 8 during the festival of the Mare de Déu de la Salut (Virgin of Health). Historically, the tradition was linked to local guilds, such as construction workers, who performed these dances as part of the town's religious processions. While the tradition dates back centuries, with roots potentially reaching the 13th century, the first concrete written record of its participation in the festival appears in the town's account books in 1733, when a stipend was paid to the musicians. By the mid-20th century, the tradition had nearly vanished, but it was successfully revived in 1973 through the efforts of local organizers and the formation of the 'Amics de la Muixeranga'.

At the heart of the Muixeranga is the performance of 'plastic' figures—human towers and tableaux that represent Marian symbols and other figurative shapes. The performance begins with the muixeranguers dancing in two rows, often carrying candles, accompanied by the hypnotic, ancient melodies of the tabalet (drum) and the dolçaina (shawm). The towers are built with a focus on technical complexity and symbolic representation rather than sheer height. A child, known as the 'enxaneta', traditionally tops the tower with open arms. The performers, who now number around 200, come from diverse professional backgrounds, though they are expected to possess strength and physical skill. The master of the group, or 'mestre', coordinates the choreography, trains new members, and directs the construction of the towers.

The costume is a distinct visual marker of the tradition, consisting of a shirt, trousers, and farmer's shoes, often featuring vertical red and blue stripes on a white base. This 'harlequin' appearance is said to have originated from the use of old mattress fabric. Beyond its aesthetic and acrobatic value, the Muixeranga is deeply embedded in the community's identity. It has been recognized by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage of humanity, reflecting its role in maintaining local culture and social cohesion. Today, the tradition has expanded beyond Algemesí, with numerous 'Noves Muixerangues' (new groups) forming across the Valencian region, ensuring the survival of this ancient, symbolic art form.

sections.origins_and_history: The tradition is rooted in the 'moixiganga', a series of human tower dances once found across the Iberian Peninsula. While some theories suggest the name derives from the Arabic 'mochain' (mask), others link it to ancient street processions. The first solemn celebrations in Algemesí occurred in 1724, and the tradition was nearly lost by 1973 before being revived by local citizens.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Performers dance in two rows before transitioning into human towers. The towers are built to form specific figurative shapes. A master coordinates the group. The movement is accompanied by the tabalet and dolçaina. Technique is focused on stability and the creation of symbolic shapes rather than competitive height.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music is played on the tabalet (drum) and the dolçaina (a loud, high-pitched shawm). The melodies are ancient and of unknown authorship, serving as a central, recognizable anthem for the tradition.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performers wear shirts and trousers with vertical red and blue stripes on a white base, reminiscent of harlequin patterns. Historically, these were made from recycled mattress fabric. The setting is the street procession during the Mare de Déu de la Salut festival.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The primary occasion is the festival of the Virgin of Health in Algemesí on September 7 and 8. It is a religious, community-based ritual that has evolved from guild-based participation to a broader social activity.
sections.notable_figures: Tomàs Pla, Martí Domínguez i Barberà, and the 1973 revival group members. Enric Cabrera is remembered as a long-term master.
sections.regional_variants: Variants include the 'Ball de Valencians' (historical), 'Els Negrets de l'Alcúdia', and various 'Noves Muixerangues' formed in the 21st century.
sections.lineage: The Muixeranga is considered the historical ancestor of the modern Catalan 'castells'.

profile.sacred_note: The Muixeranga is a religious, ritual performance dedicated to the Virgin of Health; participants and observers are expected to respect the solemnity of the processions.

basic_steps: Crowning of the tower by the child
teaching.rhythm: Traditional, rhythmic pulse set by the tabalet and dolçaina.
teaching.formation: Two rows for the initial dance, transitioning into a dense circular base for the tower.
teaching.level_notes: Requires significant physical strength, balance, and coordination; training is conducted under a master.

music_profile.sound_description: The music is defined by the piercing, high-pitched, and loud sound of the dolçaina, supported by the steady, rhythmic beat of the tabalet drum.

movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Arms are often used for balance or to support other performers; the child at the top holds arms open.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Two rows for the initial dance; dense, circular human tower for the figures.
movement_profile.partnering: High level of physical contact and trust required for building human towers.

signature_moves.name: Tower construction
signature_moves.description: Building a multi-level human structure to form a symbolic shape.

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Not described in sources, but requires professional training to avoid injury.

episode_brief.logline: Discover the ancient, gravity-defying ritual of the Muixeranga, where human bodies become living sculptures.
beats: The sound of the dolçaina signals the start of the procession.
The performers dance in two rows with candles.
The transition from dance to the construction of the human tower.
The master coordinates the base and the rising levels.
The child reaches the top, creating the final symbolic figure.
The tower descends safely, concluding the ritual.

claims.text: The costume features vertical red and blue stripes on a white base, historically made from old mattress fabric.
claims.quote: Das Gewebe ist mit vertikalen roten und blauen Streifen auf weißem Untergrund gemustert, fast wie bei einem Harlekinskostüm. Es scheint, als ob dieses merkwürdige Erscheinungsbild eher zufällig entstand, ältere Leute erinnern sich daran, dass die Kostüme früher aus dem Bezugsstoff für Matratzen gefertigt wurden.

claims.text: The tradition is recognized by UNESCO as part of the intangible heritage of humanity.
claims.quote: La muixeranga est une des traditions de la fête de la Mare de Déu de la Salut d’Algemesí qui a été inscrite en 2011 par l'UNESCO sur la liste représentative du patrimoine culturel immatériel de l'humanité.
